meta.title: Collagen Stick Buyer Benchmark
meta.description: Side-by-side comparison of nine Korean fish collagen sticks, followed by a plain-language guide to collagen, molecular size, dose, vitamin C and extra ingredients.

p1.title: Which collagen stick is best?
p1.how1: How to read the blocks. Each row scores one thing out of 10. Filled blocks = points: 8 filled blocks means 8 out of 10. Green is strong, yellow is average, orange and red are weak. The small number under each value is that row's points.
p1.how2: How the overall score is made. It is the weighted average of the four scored rows: collagen per stick (2 parts), piece size (2 parts), vitamin C (1.5 parts) and clean formula (1.5 parts). "In one box" (under each name) is information only and is not scored.
p1.foot: Data: amounts per stick calculated from each product's label (box photos, October 2026). MIPPEUM's figures and HURUM Small Molecular's 300 Da come from seller listings because they are not printed on the front of the box. Full method and sources are in the companion guide.

p2.title: What is collagen, and why do people take it?
p2.lead: Before you compare products, it helps to know what collagen is, what it does in the body and what a collagen stick is.
p2.artLabel: Two pieces of skin. Young skin has many collagen fibres. Older skin has fewer.
p2.t1: Collagen is the most common protein in the human body.<sup>1</sup> It forms long, strong threads that hold skin, bones, joints, hair and nails together.
p2.t2: In the skin, collagen threads work like the springs in a mattress. They keep skin firm, smooth and able to spring back.
p2.h3: The body makes less with age
p2.t3: As we get older, skin cells make less collagen than they did in youth.<sup>2</sup> Sun, smoking, stress and poor sleep add to this. Skin becomes thinner and drier, and lines appear.
p2.t4: A stick is a small packet with one daily serving. You mix the powder with water, or eat the jelly straight from the stick. Inside is collagen that has been cut into small pieces, called collagen peptides.
p2.t5: The body absorbs some of the small pieces into the blood.<sup>3</sup> Lab studies suggest some of them may act as a signal that tells skin cells to make more of their own collagen.<sup>4</sup> In human studies, people took collagen every day, often for 8 to 12 weeks, before results were measured.<sup>6</sup><sup>7</sup>
p2.typesTitle: There are different types of collagen. For skin, Type I matters most.
p2.ty1d: Skin, hair, nails and bones. About 90% of all collagen in the body. Comes from fish or cows. Fish collagen is mostly Type I and contains no pork or beef.
p2.ty2d: Joints and cartilage. Usually made from chicken. Used in joint products, not in skin products.
p2.ty3d: Skin and blood vessels. Works together with Type I. Usually made from cows or pigs.

p3.title: What does "Da" mean, and why is smaller better?
p3.lead: Natural collagen is a huge molecule. The body cannot absorb it whole, so makers cut it into small pieces. The Da number on the box tells you how small those pieces are.
p3.artLabel: Small collagen pieces pass through the gut wall directly. Larger pieces are first cut smaller by digestion and then absorbed.
p3.wall: Gut wall: only very small pieces fit through the gap →
p3.h1: Da is a unit of weight for molecules
p3.t1: Da is short for dalton. Scientists use it to weigh molecules, which are far too small to see. One dalton is about the weight of one hydrogen atom, the lightest atom there is. A bigger Da number means a bigger piece.
p3.h2: Collagen is a chain of beads
p3.t2: Collagen is built from small building blocks called amino acids. Picture a very long necklace: each bead is one amino acid and weighs about 100 Da. Natural collagen has about 3,000 beads, so it weighs about 300,000 Da.<sup>1</sup> Makers use enzymes to cut this necklace into short pieces.
p3.h3: Larger pieces are digested before they are absorbed
p3.t3: The gut wall takes up pieces of 2 or 3 beads (about 200–400 Da) with the help of special transporters.<sup>5</sup> Larger pieces are not wasted: digestion cuts them smaller first, and then they are absorbed too. But this takes longer, and more of the collagen ends up as single amino acids instead of the small collagen pieces found in blood in studies.<sup>3</sup>
p3.h4: The number on the box is an average
p3.t4: A box that says 300 Da means the pieces weigh 300 Da on average: most are tiny, a few are bigger. A lower average means more of the collagen is already small enough to absorb.
p3.scaleLabel: Scale: 300 Da is best, 1,000 Da is good, 2,000 Da is weak, not on the box is unknown.
p3.rule: Look for 평균분자량 (average molecular weight) on the box. 300 Da or lower is the best you can buy.
p3.slowSub: slower; more end up as single amino acids

p4.title: How much collagen is in one stick?
p4.lead: Small pieces help the body absorb collagen. But the amount matters just as much: a stick with tiny pieces and very little collagen cannot do much.
p4.artLabel: One 2 gram stick contains 2,000 mg in total; in this example 1,200 mg is collagen. Scale from 0 to 3,000 mg: under 1,000 is low, 1,000 to 2,000 is medium, over 2,000 is good. Skin studies used 2,500 mg or more a day.
p4.stickTitle: Example: one 2 g stick = 2,000 mg in total
p4.studies: Skin studies: often 2,500 mg or more
p4.t1: mg means milligram. 1,000 mg = 1 g. Stick weight is usually shown in grams, and ingredients in milligrams.
p4.h2: Not the whole stick is collagen
p4.t2: A 2 g stick weighs 2,000 mg, but part of it is flavour, vitamin C and other ingredients. Only the collagen part counts. That is why two sticks of the same weight can hold very different amounts of collagen.
p4.h3: How to find the amount on the box
p4.t3: Look for the collagen amount per stick (1포당). If the box shows only a percentage, multiply: stick weight in mg × collagen % = collagen in mg. Example: 2,000 mg × 60% = 1,200 mg. Some boxes print the total for the whole box, so check that the number is for one stick.
p4.t4: In skin studies, people often took 2,500 mg or more of collagen a day.<sup>6</sup><sup>7</sup> On our scale, under 1,000 mg per stick is low, 1,000–2,000 mg is medium and 2,000 mg or more is good.
p4.rule: Choose at least 1,000 mg of collagen per stick. 2,000 mg or more is better.

p5.title: Why vitamin C matters for collagen
p5.lead: Vitamin C does not turn into collagen. But the body cannot build collagen without it. That is why good collagen sticks include it.
p5.artLabel: Without vitamin C the collagen pieces stay in a pile. With vitamin C they are joined into a strong wall.
p5.wall: Pieces are locked into strong fibres
p5.t1: Special skin cells make new collagen fibres. They use amino acids from food and from collagen supplements as building blocks, like bricks.
p5.h2: Vitamin C is the builder's tool
p5.t2: To join the chains into a strong, stable fibre, these cells use two enzymes, and both need vitamin C to work.<sup>8</sup> Without it, the new collagen is weak and falls apart. This is why people with a severe lack of vitamin C (scurvy) get bleeding gums and wounds that do not heal.
p5.t3: The human body cannot make vitamin C and stores very little of it. We need a fresh supply every day from food or supplements.
p5.gaugeLabel: 30 mg of vitamin C covers 30% of one day's need. 100 mg covers 100%.
p5.gaugeTitle: How much of one day's vitamin C need does a stick cover?
p5.dvOther: Daily reference value: Korea 100 mg, USA 90 mg, Europe 80 mg.
p5.t4: Korea sets the daily reference value for vitamin C at 100 mg.<sup>9</sup> A stick with about 100 mg covers the full day. A stick with 30 mg covers less than a third. If vitamin C is not listed on the box, assume there is none.
p5.h5: What vitamin C does not do
p5.t5: Vitamin C does not help collagen get into the blood. Its job starts later, inside the skin, where it helps build new collagen. More than 100 mg is fine, but it does not raise the score in our ranking.
p5.rule: Look for about 100 mg of vitamin C in each stick.

p6.title: Extra ingredients: is there enough to matter?
p6.lead: Many boxes advertise extra ingredients in big letters, such as glutathione, biotin or hyaluronic acid. An ingredient can only help if there is enough of it. Below, the green circle shows the amount used in a study, and the red dot shows how much is in one stick.
p6.rule: A famous ingredient name is not a sign of quality. Check the amount in mg and compare it with the amount used in studies.

p7.title: 6 questions to ask before you buy
p7.lead: Use these questions for any collagen product, including ones not in this guide.
p7.r1: Fish collagen is mostly Type I, the type found in skin. It contains no pork or beef.
p7.q2: Is the Da printed on the box, and is it 300 Da or lower?
p7.r2: Smaller pieces are absorbed more easily. If the box does not show Da, ask the seller.
p7.q3: Is there at least 1,000 mg of collagen in one stick?
p7.r3: 2,000 mg or more is better. Skin studies often used 2,500 mg or more a day.
p7.q4: Is there about 100 mg of vitamin C in one stick?
p7.r4: The body needs vitamin C to build collagen. 100 mg covers one full day.
p7.q5: Are the extra ingredients there in useful amounts?
p7.r5: Check the mg. A famous name in a tiny amount does nothing.
p7.q6: Are the amounts shown for one stick?
p7.r6: Some boxes show the total for the whole box. Always compare one stick with one stick.
p7.disclaimer: Scores are based on the amounts printed on each product's label or seller listing. This guide compares product labels to help with buying decisions. It is not medical advice.

js.hScoreHint: weighted average of the 4 scored rows
js.glutDesc: An antioxidant that boxes often link to "whitening". In the best-known trial, adults took 250 or 1,000 mg a day for 6 months to raise glutathione levels in the body.<sup>12</sup>
js.haDesc: A substance that holds water in the skin. In the study on dry skin, people took 120 mg a day.<sup>13</sup>
js.biotinDesc: A B vitamin (vitamin B7). An adult needs about 30 µg a day.<sup>14</sup> µg means microgram: 1 mg = 1,000 µg.
js.dropText: The amount used in the study is {n} times what one stick contains. This compares amounts only; it is not a suggestion to take more sticks.
js.biotinText: One stick gives a full day of biotin, but normal food already gives enough. There is no good evidence that extra biotin improves skin or hair in people who are not lacking it.<sup>15</sup>

m.title: How the comparison sheet scores products
m.intro: Each product gets four scores out of 10, calculated from the amount in one stick. The overall score is their weighted average.
m.w1: Collagen per stick: mg ÷ 250 (2,500 mg or more = 10)
m.w2: Piece size: 300 Da or less = 10, up to 600 = 8, up to 1,000 = 6, up to 2,000 = 4, not shown = 3
m.w3: Vitamin C: mg ÷ 10 (100 mg or more = 10)
m.w4: Clean formula: our judgement of whether extras are present in useful amounts and whether the stick is mostly filler
m.data: Data come from the product labels. Where the label shows only a percentage, we multiplied it by the stick weight. MIPPEUM's figures and HURUM Small Molecular's 300 Da come from seller listings.
m.limits: Limits: we did not test the products in a laboratory. The thresholds are our own choices, guided by the studies cited in this guide. A higher score means a stronger label, not a proven effect on skin.
